title: Tinder Swindler Promises ‘Safe’ Dating App, Reveals Con Man Playbook Tactics – Fox News Exposé"}
body:
The man who turned a Tinder romance scam into a global headline is now pitching a “safer” way to meet love online. Simon Leviev—born Shimon Hayut, the Israeli‑born con artist whose lavish lifestyle and false promises of wealth were exposed in a viral documentary—has announced the upcoming launch of Safe Love, a dating platform that will reportedly rely on rigorous identity verification and blockchain‑backed credentials to block the very tactics he once used to dupe thousands.

Leviev’s re‑branding effort arrives at a moment when online‑dating fraud is soaring. A recent study by the Federal Trade Commission found that complaints about romance scams increased by 44 percent in the past year, with victims losing an estimated $1.2 billion in the United States alone. Scammers typically create convincing profiles, manipulate emotions, and then request money for travel, medical emergencies, or investment opportunities—strategies that Leviev himself mastered while posing as the son of a diamond‑magnate. By leveraging his insider knowledge of the playbook, Leviev claims Safe Love will “close the loopholes” that enable such deception.

The core of Safe Love’s promise is a multi‑layered verification process. Prospective users must submit government‑issued ID, undergo facial‑recognition matching, and link a verified payment method before they can message anyone. The company also plans to employ a decentralized ledger to store encrypted identity hashes, allowing users to confirm that a profile’s credentials have not been altered. In theory, this architecture would make it far more difficult for a fraudster to fabricate a persona or switch identities mid‑conversation.

Industry analysts, however, remain skeptical. “The technology alone won’t solve the problem,” says Dr. Maya Patel, a cybersecurity professor at the University of California, Berkeley. “Scammers are adaptable; they can still use stolen credentials, deep‑fake videos, or even recruit unwitting accomplices who have already passed verification.” Moreover, the requirement for extensive personal data raises privacy concerns. Critics point out that a platform built around identity confirmation could become a lucrative target for data breaches, potentially exposing users to a different set of risks.

Legal experts also note the potential regulatory hurdles. In the European Union, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) imposes strict limits on how personal data can be collected, stored, and shared. Safe Love would need to demonstrate a lawful basis for processing sensitive information and provide users with clear rights to delete or port their data. In the United States, state‑level privacy statutes such as California’s Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) could further complicate compliance, especially if the app expands globally.

Despite the challenges, the venture has attracted notable venture‑capital interest. A seed round reportedly raised $7 million from investors who see a market gap for “trust‑first” dating services. Leviev’s own narrative—transitioning from a convicted fraudster to a tech entrepreneur championing consumer protection—has generated both curiosity and controversy, fueling media coverage that may serve as free advertising for the fledgling platform.

If Safe Love can deliver on its security promises without compromising user privacy, it could set a new benchmark for the industry, prompting competitors to adopt similar verification standards. Conversely, failure to protect data or prevent sophisticated fraud could reinforce skepticism about tech‑driven solutions to deeply human problems. As the app moves toward a beta launch later this year, users and regulators alike will be watching closely to see whether a man who once exploited trust can now help rebuild it.
